| [THEORY-028](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-028.md) v2 | The expected bias of any data-dependent choice, and the expected generalisation error of any learning algorithm, is at most √(2σ²·I) for σ-subgaussian losses, where I is the information the output carries about the data | Russo & Zou (2015), [LIT-356](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-356.md), Prop. 1: \|E[φ_T − µ_T]\| ≤ σ√(2·I(T;φ)) for any selection T among σ-sub-Gaussian statistics. | [THEORY-032](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-032.md) | The Yoneda lemma determines an object only up to isomorphism, from its whole hom-functor, among objects the category already has; as a formal version of "an object is determined by its relations" it presupposes the relata | nLab, Yoneda lemma (rev. 2026-08-17), [LIT-221](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-221.md) — y is fully faithful and y(c) ≅ y(d) iff c ≅ d, and pointwise bijections of hom-sets without naturality do not suffice. | [THEORY-041](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-041.md) | Birkhoff and von Neumann proposed the modular law, not orthomodularity, and proved it fails for closed subspaces in infinite dimension; Husimi used the orthomodular identity only as an unnamed proof step | Birkhoff & von Neumann (1936), [LIT-306](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-306.md) — the lattice of closed subspaces is orthocomplemented and not distributive. | [THEORY-053](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-053.md) | A treatment's efficacy is not evidence for its theory of change: only change in the theorised process that is specific and comes before the outcome bears on it, and moving the process without moving the outcome counts against the theory | Salkovskis, Sighvatsson and Sigurdsson ([LIT-538](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-538.md)): "The effectiveness of a treatment is not evidence for the validity of the theory on which it is based", with one exception, that changing the theory's crucial factor without changing the problem disconfirms it. | [THEORY-066](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-066.md) | A Markov-blanket partition is defined relative to a chosen internal set, so a graph has one around almost any set of nodes, and the formalism alone does not say which set is the system | The formal core of Bruineberg et al.'s critique ([LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md), C4 in [NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)). In a directed acyclic graph the blanket of a node set A is its parents, children and the children's other parents, and A is conditionally independent of everything outside A and its blanket. That holds for every A, so any set whose blanket leaves something outside gets a valid internal, blanket and external partition. Having a blanket therefore picks out no set. In Friston's soup ([LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md)) the set was picked by spectral clustering with k = 8, not by the blanket. Active because it is a short derivation that anyone can check. It covers graphical (Pearl) blankets and the 2013 procedure. It does not cover the later sparse-coupling definitions at nonequilibrium steady state, which the record has not read. | Active |
| [THEORY-068](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-068.md) | In a two-alternative choice made by two competing leaky accumulators, the decision is optimal only when leak and mutual inhibition balance, so that the network integrates the difference of the evidence without loss; imbalance bounds accuracy at any fixed time and weights early or late evidence | Bogacz et al. | [THEORY-081](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-081.md) v2 | The evidence of any model formed from a full model by changing only its prior is the full evidence times the full posterior expectation of the prior ratio, so the Savage–Dickey ratio is its point-mass case and choosing which parameters to keep is evidence maximisation over the prior | Friston & Penny (2011), [LIT-620](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-620.md), Eq. 3: if models share a likelihood and differ only in priors nested inside a full prior, then p(y\|m_i) = p(y\|m_F)·E_{p(θ\|y,m_F)}[p_i(θ)/p_F(θ)]. | [THEORY-082](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-082.md) | Steepest descent is defined only relative to a metric, and Amari's proof that natural-gradient learning is Fisher efficient needs the Fisher information at the optimum to be invertible, the condition whose failure WBIC calls singular; in a multilayer perceptron it fails wherever an output weight is zero | Amari (1998), [LIT-607](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-607.md). Theorem 1 is a Lagrangian derivation: under \|dw\|² = Σg_ij dw_i dw_j the steepest-descent direction is −G⁻¹∇L, so it changes with G. Theorem 2 shows that online learning with step 1/t along the Fisher natural gradient attains the Cramér–Rao bound G⁻¹/t, and its proof uses G(w*)⁻¹. Watanabe, [LIT-616](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-616.md), Eq. 14, calls a truth regular when the optimum is one point and its Fisher is positive definite, and singular otherwise. From Amari's own Eq. 6.12, the score for hidden unit i's input weights carries the factor v_i. So the Fisher of a multilayer perceptron loses rank wherever an output weight is zero. That set is part of the optimum whenever the teacher needs fewer hidden units than the student has. Active because each step is checkable in the two texts. The claim that the Fisher is the only invariant metric is Chentsov's, cited and not held. | Active |

| [THEORY-121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-121.md) v4 | Moral responsibility requires guidance control, moderate reasons-responsiveness of the agent's own actual-sequence mechanism, and not regulative control over alternative possibilities, so responsibility is compatible with causal determinism | Fischer and Ravizza, in their own précis ([LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md), read): moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. | [THEORY-132](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-132.md) | Stability, a system's speed of return to equilibrium after disturbance, and resilience, its capacity to absorb change and persist within its domain of attraction, are distinct properties that can trade off, so a system can be highly unstable and highly resilient, and managing it for constancy can erode its resilience | Holling (1973), [LIT-741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-741.md). Stability is return to equilibrium. Resilience is persistence under change, set by the extent of the domain of attraction and the system's distance from its edge. Budworm forests and insect populations in harsh climates are unstable and resilient; homogeneous lakes are stable and fragile. Active for the distinction, which has become standard. The claim that management for constancy erodes resilience rests on suggestive cases. | Active |
| [THEORY-134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-134.md) | Whether a system can persist is a question about a constraint set fixed independently of its dynamics: a set is viable when from each of its states some evolution can stay in it, and when it is not, its viability kernel is the largest part that is, from the rest of which every evolution leaves in finite time | Aubin's viability theory, read in his 1999 mini-course notes [LIT-714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-714.md). Given dynamics and a set K of required states, K is viable if some evolution from each state stays in K and invariant if every one does. Nagumo's theorem reduces viability to a tangency condition. The viability kernel is the largest viable subset of K; from outside it every evolution exits K. The notes do not compare viability with stability; that contrast is a further step. | Active |
| [THEORY-136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-136.md) v2 | A persistent or abrupt change is not evidence that a system has alternative stable states: field patterns such as jumps, multimodality and dual relationships also arise from a stepwise driver or a simple threshold, and only hysteresis, initial-state dependence or a lasting shift after a temporary disturbance, with slow return excluded, comes close to showing one | Scheffer & Carpenter (2003), [LIT-726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-726.md). Alternative attractors predict sudden shifts, multimodal states and dual responses to a driver, and so do discontinuous drivers and threshold responses. Discriminating evidence is experimental: different starting states reaching different end states, temporary disturbances causing lasting shifts, or hysteresis. Slow recovery can mimic all three. Positive feedback must be strong to produce alternative states. Active as a methodological standard. | Active |
| [THEORY-138](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-138.md) | X is a cause of Y exactly when some intervention on X with respect to Y would change Y, where an intervention is an exogenous causal process that alone sets X (M1), affects Y only through X (M2), is not caused by anything that affects Y by another route (M3), and leaves Y's causes off the path through X unchanged (M4); so defined, causation is not reduced to non-causal facts but is not viciously circular, and needs no human agent | Woodward, "Causation and Manipulability" (SEP, 2001; revised 2023), [LIT-713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-713.md). A cause is what changes the effect under a surgical, exogenous intervention, defined relative to the effect by M1–M4. The account separates total from direct causes by combining interventions, and treats natural experiments as interventions. Active as the standard the record uses for what a causal claim asserts. This statement says nothing about invariance, proportionality or levels. | Active |
| [THEORY-149](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-149.md) | Users can govern a shared resource durably without either privatisation or central control, and the institutions that last are marked not by particular rules but by structural regularities: user-made and user-monitored rules, graduated sanctions, cheap local conflict resolution, recognised rights to self-organise, and nested layers of governance | Ostrom's account, read in her Nobel lecture ([LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md)). Coded case meta-analyses, laboratory and field experiments and multi-country field studies agree that resource users often self-govern successfully. Long-surviving institutions share eight design principles that failed ones lack. The principles are correlates of survival, not tested causes, and their reach beyond common-pool resources is not shown. | Active |
| [THEORY-215](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-215.md) | A Hawkes process with a Lipschitz rate function and signed kernels has a unique stationary regime, which suitably started versions approach, when the Lipschitz-weighted absolute kernel mass is below one (a spectral radius below one, for a network) or when the rate is bounded | Brémaud and Massoulié (1996), [LIT-1035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1035.md), read in [NOTE-728](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-728.md): Theorems 1, 2, 7 and 8, proved. Inhibition is allowed because the conditions use \|h\|. The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; the kernels are fixed in time; uniqueness is among solutions with finite mean intensity. In the linear excitatory case the condition is the branching ratio below one, but in the nonlinear signed case the spectral-radius quantity is a bound, not a branching ratio, and a bounded rate needs no bound on the kernels at all. Nothing is proved about cascade sizes or about what happens past the threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-260](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-260.md) v3 | An individual string's information splits non-trivially into structure and noise only in a model class without a universal member: with partial recursive models every string's minimal sufficient statistic is trivial, while with total recursive functions it is not, and the finite-set, computable-distribution and total-function classes agree to within logarithmic terms | Vitányi (2001/2006), [LIT-229](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-229.md), read in [NOTE-790](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-790.md). | [THEORY-337](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-337.md) | In the comparative-question paradigm, judging whether a quantity is higher or lower than a high or low anchor pulls the later estimate of it toward the anchor, with large effects in five preregistered experiments of 128 people each, lasting through dozens of intervening word-recognition trials | Harris et al. In five preregistered experiments (N = 128 each) on temperatures and car prices, estimates after a high anchor exceeded those after a low one every time (d ≈ 0.85–1.39), with 40 to 70 word-recognition trials between the comparison and the estimate. Strack and Mussweiler's three small studies show the same effect, and that it can shrink or reverse when the knowledge used to compare does not apply to the estimate. This is the effect, not its mechanism: why the estimate moves is [THEORY-335](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-335.md)'s question and is not settled. | Active |
| [THEORY-338](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-338.md) | For a list searched from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each found item to the front costs at most twice what any rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the future (four times counting its own moves), a fixed order by access frequency is within no constant factor, and paying to rearrange ahead of need never helps; for paging, no online rule beats the offline optimum by less than n/(n − n_MIN + 1), and LRU meets that bound | Sleator and Tarjan (1985), [LIT-1093](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1093.md), read in [NOTE-903](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-903.md). With no probabilistic assumption, move-to-front on a sequentially scanned list is within 2 of the best algorithm in its class on every sequence, the rival being free to rearrange as it goes and to know the whole future; a list sorted once by frequency, transpose and frequency count are not within any constant; and any algorithm can be replaced by one no more expensive that makes no paid rearrangement (Theorem 3). For paging the online price of not knowing the future is n/(n − n_MIN + 1), the size of fast memory when the memories are equal. It is one list, or one two-level memory, with uniform items: it says nothing about bins, partitions or search that is not a scan. | Active |
| [THEORY-340](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-340.md) | For answering membership in a static set of n keys with the fewest worst-case cell reads, sorted order with binary search is optimal only when the key universe exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold and table cells may hold nothing but stored keys or pointer symbols; it is beaten for small universes, and by two probes once one cell may hold an encoded value | Yao (1981), [LIT-1097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1097.md), read in [NOTE-891](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-891.md). In the setting later called the cell-probe model, where only cells read are counted and both the arrangement and the adaptive search are arbitrary, ⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes are needed by any scheme whose cells hold only keys of the set or a fixed stock of pointer symbols, once the universe is astronomically large (Theorems 1 and 1′). One probe suffices for m ≤ 2n − 2 (Theorem 2), and with one extra cell holding any value two probes suffice for m ≥ 2^{16n²} (Theorem 3). Building the table is free, so the paper prices lookup only and says nothing about whether sorting pays for itself. | Active |
| [THEORY-341](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-341.md) | Inferring not-P from failure to prove P is a deduction only under two separate conditions: Clark shows that when every branch of the search for a proof of P ends in failure, not-P is a theorem of the completed database, and a search that does not finish licenses nothing; Reiter's closed-world assumption, adding the negation of every ground atom the database does not entail, keeps a consistent Horn database consistent and can make a disjunctive one inconsistent | Clark (1978), [LIT-1087](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1087.md), read in [NOTE-894](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-894.md), and Reiter (1978), [LIT-1088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1088.md), read in [NOTE-899](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-899.md) from his 1977 workshop report. Clark proves negation as failure sound with respect to the completed database (the clauses read as if-and-only-if definitions, plus axioms that distinct names denote distinct things), given a finite failure tree for some selection rule; it is incomplete in general. Reiter defines the closed-world assumption by entailment, reduces closed-world query evaluation to open-world atomic queries when the assumption is consistent, and shows it consistent for Horn and definite databases but not for Pa ∨ Pb. Soundness here is relative to the completion, not to the world, and neither paper says anything about a search cut short by time. | Active |
| [THEORY-345](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-345.md) | Choosing indexes for a known mix of queries and updates, to minimize query cost plus a per-index upkeep, is NP-hard as the number of attributes and query types grows, and the tools built for it choose one stored order and a set of secondary indexes per table by searching configurations costed with the query optimizer's own estimates, optimal at best relative to those estimates, with no proved guarantee for their heuristics and no term for the one-time cost of building | Piatetsky-Shapiro (1983), [LIT-1089](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1089.md), read in [NOTE-902](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-902.md); Finkelstein, Schkolnick and Tiberio (1988), [LIT-1084](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1084.md), read in [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md); Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md), read in [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md). Minimum set cover reduces to choosing single-attribute secondary indexes under a known workload with a fixed upkeep per index. DBDSGN chooses the one clustered order and the secondary indexes per table against a frequency-weighted sum of access, update and upkeep costs plus storage, read from the System R optimizer; AutoAdmin picks at most k indexes by greedy search over what-if indexes. The model is steady state over a fixed workload: it prices upkeep against per-query savings, not a one-off build or sort against later lookups, and its optimality is relative to the optimizer's estimates, never to measured execution. | Active |
| [THEORY-346](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-346.md) | When information stays in view at a known place, people consult it less and rely on memory more as the time to reach it rises, in a graded trend across added delays from 0 to 3.2 seconds, even where the memory is weak and the display perfect; in one copying task a model that prices memory and display access in time alone, with no preference for either source, fits how many items people encode per look | Gray, Sims, Fu and Schoelles (2006), [LIT-1073](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1073.md), read in [NOTE-868](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-868.md), and Gray and Fu (2004), [LIT-1058](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1058.md), read in [NOTE-864](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-864.md). Adding a click to reach on-screen show information cut how often it was checked, and checks of finished settings came from memory. Lockouts of 0 to 3,200 ms on a Blocks World pattern cut looks and raised blocks placed per look, with linear trends. An ideal performer model with ACT-R memory equations and Q-learning on time alone fits four measures. That the control system has no bias toward the world is argued, not tested against a rival model. Errors in the 2004 study differed only against a group that memorized under several other changes, and the 2006 model has no wrong retrievals, no precomputation, no reuse across trials and no staleness. | Active |
| [THEORY-347](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-347.md) | Belief bases with the same logical closure can revise to opposite conclusions on the same input, so a closed belief set does not fix its own revision; partial meet contraction of a base need not satisfy Recovery, and bases keep distinct inconsistent states apart, while a belief-set model reproduces the base difference only by attaching a different selection mechanism to the same set | Hansson's Stanford Encyclopedia survey (2006, revised 2026), [LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md), read in [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md), with Alchourrón, Gärdenfors and Makinson (1985), [LIT-1050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1050.md), read in [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md). Bases {p, q} and {p, p ↔ q} have one closure, yet revised by ¬p one yields q and the other ¬q: statically but not dynamically equivalent. Base contraction escapes the Recovery that AGM proves for closed theories, and many inconsistent bases exist where there is one inconsistent closed set. A base marks which beliefs are held in their own right and recomputes the rest; it is not a record of reasons, sources or defeated alternatives, and the survey gives no result that bases handle iterated revision better. | Active |
| [THEORY-348](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-348.md) | When staying in one state costs a fixed amount per request and leaving it costs a fixed one-time price, switching once the extra cost paid for staying equals that price is within 2 of the offline optimum on every request sequence, and no deterministic online rule does better; with a third option the best guaranteed ratio rises to 3 | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph and Sleator (1988), [LIT-1096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1096.md), read in [NOTE-893](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-893.md). A snoopy cache holding a shared block pays 1 per write to keep it current, or drops it and pays p to fetch it again on a later read. Dropping once the writes charged since the last read have cost p is strongly 2-competitive (Theorems 3.1 and 4.1); with a read- or write-through option the deterministic lower bound is 3 (Theorem 3.3). It is the first competitive analysis of a rent-or-buy decision, though the paper never uses the name, and its instance is when to stop maintaining a copy. Prices are fixed and known, the guarantee is worst case only, stale reads are forbidden rather than priced, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Active |
| [THEORY-349](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-349.md) | For binary outcomes and a fixed representation of individuals, a predictor can pass every test in a bounded class without being close to nature: outcome indistinguishability to tests that see the sampled prediction is equivalent, with stated losses, to multicalibration over a closely related class of sets, a predictor meeting it exists at size polynomial in the tests' size and the tolerance whatever nature's complexity, and learning one is as hard as weak agnostic learning of the class | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md), and Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold and Rothblum (2018), [LIT-1052](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1052.md), read in [NOTE-879](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-879.md). A predictor is outcome indistinguishable relative to a class of distinguishers when none can tell nature's outcomes from outcomes drawn from the predictor, up to ε. With no access or sample access to the predictor this is equivalent to multi-accuracy or multicalibration over closely related classes, and a predictor meeting it exists at size O(s/ε²) (O(s/α⁴γ) for multicalibration), independent of nature. Learning a multicalibrated predictor is equivalent to weak agnostic learning of the class. Adequacy here is relative to the class, the outcome and the features, and is not unique; it is not closeness to the truth, and the papers say nothing about signal detection. | Active |
| [THEORY-350](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-350.md) | Under a budget on maintenance time, a stored view's upkeep depends on which other views are stored, so upkeep is not additive and adding a view can lower it, and greedily adding the single view of best saving per unit of upkeep can be arbitrarily bad; on OR view graphs a greedy over inverted tree sets gets 1 − 1/e of the saving of an optimum given as much upkeep, using up to twice the budget, if no tree-piece of the optimum alone exceeds the budget | Gupta and Mumick (1999), [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md), read in [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md), with the proofs of the journal version (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md), and the superadditivity first noted by Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md). Minimizing query cost subject to a cap on total maintenance time, one stored view can make another cheaper to keep current, so saving per unit of upkeep is not monotone and single-view greedy fails without bound (Example 2). Grouping views into inverted tree sets restores a 1 − 1/e guarantee, proved in 2005 (Theorem 8), for OR view graphs only, bicriteria, under an assumption on the optimum, with greedy stages exponential in general. The proof does not treat the negative effective costs the paper allows. Upkeep is a budget, not a cost traded against savings, and staleness and build cost are not modelled. | Active |
| [THEORY-352](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-352.md) | A pseudorandom generator exists if and only if a one-way function exists, where both are secure against uniform adversaries and every reduction is an oracle Turing machine, as statements about ensembles indexed by n; the construction from an arbitrary one-way function is only weak-preserving, so security at one length is bought at a much greater one | Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby (1999), [LIT-1051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1051.md), read in [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md), with Goldreich's Foundations of Cryptography, [LIT-1061](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1061.md), skimmed in [NOTE-863](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-863.md) from the 1995 draft. Theorem 6.2.2: "There are one-way functions iff there are pseudorandom generators." The hard direction runs one-way function → false entropy generator → pseudoentropy generator → generator, by uniform reductions, with seeds of length n^10 in the direct construction. Adversaries are algorithms; the paper has no circuit version, and that the proof carries over to non-uniform adversaries is the reading's inference, not the paper's statement. Everything is asymptotic. Goldreich states the theorem and does not prove it. | Active |
| [THEORY-353](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-353.md) | For a logically closed theory, the contractions satisfying the six basic AGM postulates are exactly the partial meet contractions, and those satisfying the two supplementary postulates as well are exactly the ones whose selection of remainders is generated by a transitive relation; the theory alone does not fix the contraction, and the results concern one change of one fixed theory | Alchourrón, Gärdenfors and Makinson (1985), [LIT-1050](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1050.md), read in [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md), with Hansson's survey, [LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md), read in [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md). Contracting a closed theory A by x keeps what a selected set of maximal x-free subsets of A share; the six basic postulates characterize exactly these partial meet contractions (Observation 2.5), and with the two supplementary postulates exactly those selected by a transitive relation (Corollary 4.5). Revision follows by the Levi identity. A selection function or ordering must be added to A, and in the finite case distinct ones give distinct contractions. Nothing here concerns iterated change, where the selection comes from, or why a belief is held. | Active |
| [THEORY-354](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-354.md) | An observer's power to refute a predictor depends on its access to the predictor as well as on its budget: against tests that see only the sampled prediction a predictor of size O(s/ε²) always passes, but if fine-grained clique counting is hard, or BPP ≠ PSPACE, some cheap tests that may query the predictor adaptively pass only predictors about as costly as nature's own | Dwork, Kim, Reingold, Rothblum and Yona (2021), [LIT-1068](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1068.md), read in [NOTE-885](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-885.md). Against sample-access distinguishers of size s an outcome-indistinguishable predictor of size O(s/ε²) always exists. Against oracle-access distinguishers, under fine-grained hardness of clique counting or BPP ≠ PSPACE, there are natures and polynomially many cheap distinguishers such that no predictor much cheaper than nature is indistinguishable. Non-adaptive queries add little; the power comes from adaptive queries. The results are conditional and asymptotic, with upper and lower bounds in different parameterisations; they say nothing about human observers or about which access a real auditor has. | Active |
| [THEORY-356](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-356.md) | When stored views are never updated, greedily storing the view of largest marginal saving in query cost gets at least 1 − 1/e of the optimal saving on a data-cube lattice or any OR or AND view graph, against the optimum for the same number of views or for the space the greedy ends up using, which may exceed the budget by one view | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md), read in [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md); Gupta (1997), [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md), read in [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md); Gupta and Mumick (2005), [LIT-1080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1080.md), read in [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md). A stored answer is worth the saving on every query derivable from it, less what answers already stored save, and greedy on that marginal saving gets 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ 1 − 1/e of the best saving for k views; under a space budget the same holds against the optimum in the space the greedy actually uses (up to one view over), or 0.63 − f when no view takes more than a fraction f of the budget. The bound is on saving against storing the base view alone, not on query cost, and it holds only with no updates: once upkeep enters the objective it is proved only for AND graphs in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. | Active |
| [THEORY-357](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-357.md) | Computational indistinguishability is strictly coarser than statistical closeness: without any assumption there are ensembles on at most 2^(n/2) strings that no circuit of size 2^(n/8) tells from uniform, though none of them is efficiently samplable, and an efficiently samplable pair of this kind exists if a pseudorandom generator does, since its output covers at most 2^n of the 2^l(n) strings; all of it is about ensembles indexed by n, not single pairs of distributions | Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography vol. 1, [LIT-1061](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1061.md), read in [NOTE-863](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-863.md) (Skimmed, 1995 draft, Chapters 1–3 in full), with Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby (1999), [LIT-1051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1051.md), read in [NOTE-880](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-880.md). Proposition 3.3 proves by counting that some ensemble far from uniform fools every small circuit; its proof is non-constructive and the ensemble cannot be sampled efficiently. A generator's output is efficiently samplable, indistinguishable from uniform by definition, and statistically far by an image count (§3.3.1). That a samplable such pair exists only if one-way functions do is cited to Goldreich 1990, not read. The book's statistical difference has no factor ½, so it is twice total variation. | Active |
| [THEORY-358](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-358.md) | In visual search among up to about 36 well-spaced items, a target that alone carries one colour or one distinctive shape part is found in time almost independent of the number of items, while a target identified only by a combination of features its neighbours carry separately takes time that grows linearly with the number of items, about twice as fast when the target is absent, the pattern of a serial self-terminating scan, and practice did not remove it; that conjunctions rather than similarity cause it is the paper's reading, not its result | Treisman and Gelade (1980), [LIT-1082](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1082.md), read in [NOTE-897](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-897.md). With coloured letters on cards of 1 to 30 or 36 items, a blue letter or an S among brown Ts and green Xs was found at 3.8 and 2.5 ms per item, and a green T among the same distractors at 28.7 ms per item when present and 67.1 when absent, linear and in the ratio of a scan that stops at the first find; 13 sessions of practice did not change it. The paper reads the contrast as feature integration: conjunction structure, not similarity, makes search serial. That reading is contested by the similarity account of Duncan and Humphreys ([LIT-1081](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1081.md)), which the record could not obtain, and it does not follow that any item unique in one attribute pops out in a real pile. | Active |
| [THEORY-361](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-361.md) | When every object but one has full grade in exactly one of two attribute-sorted lists and the one has full grade in both, finding it under min takes at least about half the objects' worth of accesses for any algorithm that only reads the lists from the top and looks up objects already seen, and, with the tied objects in random order, about as many in expectation even for algorithms that may look up any object; a query on one attribute alone costs k accesses whatever the number of objects | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): Example 6.3 and Theorem 6.4, the paper's proof that no algorithm is instance optimal once lucky lookups are allowed. With 2n + 1 objects, n + 1 high in each list and only one high in both, an algorithm that cannot guess must read at least n + 1 entries before it sees the target, and on a randomized family any deterministic algorithm needs at least n + 1 accesses in expectation. The paper uses the case to bound instance optimality. That it explains linear conjunction-search slopes in human vision is the record's analogy, not the paper's claim. | Active |
| [THEORY-363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-363.md) | For finding the top k objects under a monotone combining function from m lists each sorted by one attribute, with sorted and random accesses the only costs, the threshold algorithm is correct and on every database costs at most a constant times what any correct algorithm that makes no wild guesses costs; the constant is m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, no deterministic algorithm does better when the function is strict, and once wild guesses are allowed no algorithm has such a guarantee on databases with ties | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). The threshold algorithm reads m attribute-sorted lists in parallel, looks up each new object's other grades, and stops when k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. For every monotone combining function it is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no wild guesses (Theorem 6.1), with ratio m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, tight for strict functions (Corollary 6.2, Theorem 9.1). It is a guarantee relative to a class of algorithms under an access-cost model. It does not say that top-k queries are cheap: the absolute cost depends on the data, and is linear in N for some conjunctive queries. | Active |
| [THEORY-364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-364.md) | When each cached value is an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, and a query must return an answer interval no wider than R whatever the true values, choosing the cheapest set of exact reads for a SUM is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and solved by taking the narrowest intervals first when read costs are equal, and for a COUNT with a selection predicate the cheapest choice is the ⌈\|T?\| − R⌉ cheapest undecided tuples | Olston and Widom (2000), [LIT-1117](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1117.md), read in [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md). In TRAPP a cache holds intervals that sources keep valid by pushing a refresh whenever a value escapes, and each query names a width R its answer may have. The SUM answer is the sum of the intervals, so meeting R at least read cost is knapsack (profit = read cost, weight = width, capacity = R); COUNT under a predicate has a greedy optimum. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and only the query-time cost of buying it down is optimized: the sources' upkeep, the choice of interval widths and any cost of imprecision are outside the model. The MIN rule's optimality proof is in an unread technical report. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. Theorem 1: for n fixed data points and an independent query, var(d^p / E[d^p]) → 0 implies P[DMAX ≤ (1+ε)DMIN] → 1 for every ε > 0. The index m is arbitrary, so dimension enters only through the workload's distance distributions. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |
| [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). Proved for the two-dimensional lattice: with nodes, local links and the number of long-range links fixed, changing only the exponent r of the long-range link distribution moves the expected delivery time of the best decentralized searcher from O((log n)²) at r = 2 to a power of n at every other r, including r = 0, where paths of polylogarithmic length exist. The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-371](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-371.md) | For conjunctive queries without equality or comparisons, two queries are equivalent exactly when homomorphisms run both ways between the queries read as small databases, every such query has a minimal equivalent query unique up to isomorphism obtained by deleting atoms, and evaluating one against a database is NP-complete when the query is part of the input | Chandra and Merlin (1977), [LIT-1111](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1111.md), read in [NOTE-907](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-907.md). Reading a conjunctive query as its natural model, equivalence becomes a pair of homomorphisms (Lemma 13), the minimal equivalent query is unique up to isomorphism (Theorem 12), and evaluation with the query as input is NP-complete (Theorem 7), as is deciding whether one query is a folding of another (Theorem 11). The paper states equivalence, not containment, and does not state that containment or equivalence is NP-complete; those are corollaries later work attributes to it. Nothing here reaches queries with equality, comparisons, negation or union. | Active |
| [THEORY-372](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-372.md) | For c-approximate near-neighbour search over n points in Euclidean space, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} are achievable on any data set whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming space), and no list-of-points structure, the model of known data-independent hashing, does better on random instances; without that model the curve is matched only at query time n^{o(1)} by one or two cell probes | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten (2017), [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md), read in [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) from the arXiv full version. A data-dependent tree of spherical caps, with different thresholds for filing points and for routing queries, realizes every pair of exponents on the curve, for worst-case data, with constant success probability; the equal-threshold point is LSH. On random instances with d = ω(log n), list-of-points structures cannot beat the curve (a lower bound the paper calls conditional), and one- or two-probe cell-probe structures need n^{(c/(c−1))²−o(1)} words, the curve's space at ρq = 0. Optimality for data-dependent schemes, for more probes, and for d = Θ(log n) is not shown. The curve prices space against per-query time for one query at a time; it has no workload and no build cost beyond space. | Active |
| [THEORY-373](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-373.md) | For positive relational algebra on relations whose tuples are annotated from a commutative semiring, every query's annotated answer equals its answer over provenance polynomials N[X] in the input tuple ids, evaluated at the input annotations, so set, bag, c-table and event-table semantics all factor through the polynomials; revaluing inputs can remove output tuples but never add them, and nothing is shown for negation, difference or aggregation | Green, Karvounarakis and Tannen (2007), [LIT-1110](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1110.md), read in [NOTE-913](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-913.md). Union and projection add tags, join multiplies them; the usual RA identities hold exactly when the tags form a commutative semiring, and a map of tags commutes with every query exactly when it is a semiring homomorphism. The polynomials N[X] are the free commutative semiring, so the annotated answer in any semiring is the polynomial answer evaluated at the input annotations (Theorem 4.3). It is a sufficiency result for revisions that re-annotate existing inputs, not a minimality result, and it excludes added facts and every nonmonotone operation. | Active |
| [THEORY-378](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-378.md) | When items change as independent Poisson processes with known rates and a fixed total refresh rate is shared among them, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy at least as fresh and at most as old, averaged over time, as refreshing in proportion to change rate, for any spread of rates; the freshness-optimal share rises and then falls with change rate and gives nothing to items that change too fast for the budget | Cho and Garcia-Molina (2000), [LIT-1119](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1119.md), read in [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md). Freshness is the fraction of items equal to their source, age the mean time since an unseen change, both averaged over time and over equally weighted items. With fixed-interval refresh, uniform refresh is never worse than proportional on either measure, by convexity (proof in the authors' technical report). Under a fixed budget the freshness-optimal allocation starves the fastest-changing items; the age-optimal one refreshes them somewhat more. It prices staleness as an objective under a fixed budget: there are no reads, no query savings, no build cost and no cost of a stale use, so it is a staleness term and not a model trading staleness against upkeep. | Active |
| [THEORY-381](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-381.md) | In the cell-probe model, a near-neighbour structure on n random points that answers in t probes with m cells of w bits must satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ the robust expansion of the metric's neighbourhood graph at measure 1/m^t (and (mwt/n)^t ≥ its vertex expansion if deterministic), so in expanding spaces such as the hypercube fast queries need space polynomially larger than the data; the bounds are average case, approximate, and fall off exponentially in t | Panigrahy, Talwar and Wieder (2010), [LIT-1102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1102.md), read in [NOTE-914](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-914.md) from the arXiv preprint. For graphical neighbour search, to which decision approximate near neighbour reduces, on data drawn so that neighbourhoods rarely overlap: deterministic t-probe structures satisfy (mwt/n)^t ≥ Φv and m^t·t·w/n ≥ Φv(1/m^t); randomized ones satisfy m^t·w/n ≥ Φr(1/m^t, γ/t) and (mwt⁴/n)^{2t} ≥ Φr(1/m, γ/t). On the hypercube this gives space n^{1+Ω(1/(ct))} at approximation c and n^{Ω(1/(tε²))} at 1 + ε; a one-probe structure matches on Cayley graphs; low-contention dynamic structures need update time at least Φr(τ, 1/(4t²)) over poly(t). Tight only for constant t; nothing about worst-case or structured data, workloads or build time. | Active |
| [THEORY-384](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-384.md) | A nearest-neighbour graph built by pruning each point's links against all other points with a factor α > 1, so that from every point some link is α times closer to any other point, lets greedy search from any start reach a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by one on n, and the build takes O(n³) time done naively | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). Proved for DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" build, not the build DiskANN implements. The guarantee rests on one property of the graph (α-shortcut reachability, α > 1), gives a constant approximation, not exact search, is logarithmic in the aspect ratio ∆, which can exceed n by far, and has a per-step cost exponential in the doubling dimension. HNSW and NSG prune with α = 1 and are not covered. | Active |
| [THEORY-386](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-386.md) | When a cached interval of width W is kept valid by its source, which pushes a refresh at cost C_vr whenever the value leaves it, and queries fetch the exact value at cost C_qr whenever it is too wide, and the chances of the two per step go as 1/W² and as W, the expected refresh cost is least at W* = (ρK₁/K₂)^(1/3) with ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, where ρ times the chance of a pushed refresh equals the chance of a fetch | Olston, Loo and Widom (2001), [LIT-1109](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1109.md), read in [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md). The cost rate Ω(W) = C_vr·K₁/W² + C_qr·K₂·W is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr. The minimum is calculus on assumed forms. P_qr ∝ W follows exactly from uniform precision demands; P_vr ∝ 1/W² comes from a Chebyshev bound on a random walk used as an estimate, and the paper's simulation of a random walk measured both proportionalities. Staleness here is priced as refresh traffic: the source guarantees validity, so a stale read is imprecise but never wrong, and there is no build cost and no cost of a wrong or imprecise answer. | Active |
| [THEORY-388](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-388.md) | Locality-sensitive hashing answers approximate near-neighbour queries over n points with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, where ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) is set by how much more often near pairs collide than far ones and is at most 1/(1+ε) for approximation 1+ε in Hamming space, with constant success probability per query; the paper gives upper bounds only and proves no limit on what organizing can buy | Indyk and Motwani (1998), [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md), read in [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) from the authors' 1999 expanded version, compared with the STOC text. A hash family under which points within r1 collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond r2 with at most p2 gives n^ρ random tables, each storing every point: O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), for the decision version, which ring-cover trees connect to approximate nearest neighbour with polylog overhead. Bit sampling gives ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in Hamming space and, by embedding, ℓ_p for p in [1, 2]; the STOC text states 1/ε and only for ε > 1. Grid bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Preprocessing is counted as space. Nothing is proved about whether these exponents can be beaten. | Active |
| [THEORY-389](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-389.md) | For conjunctive queries and views without comparison predicates, a stored view can be used in an equivalent rewriting of a query exactly when the view's body maps homomorphically into the query's, a minimal rewriting needs no more literals than the query, and deciding whether a rewriting shorter than the query or one using only the views exists is NP-complete in the size of the query and view definitions; with comparisons in both, deciding whether any rewriting uses the views is Π2p-complete | Levy, Mendelzon, Sagiv and Srivastava (1995), [LIT-1100](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1100.md), read in [NOTE-909](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-909.md). Every use of a view in an equivalent rewriting comes from a containment mapping from the view into the query (Proposition 3.1); without comparisons a locally minimal complete rewriting has at most as many literals as the query (Lemma 3.5), which puts the problems in NP, and they are NP-complete (Theorems 3.7, 3.9, 3.10), with two independent sources of hardness. The results are worst case, in the size of the definitions rather than the stored data, for equivalent rewritings under set semantics only; they do not say recognizing reuse is costly in practice, and they do not cover contained (partial) rewritings. | Active |
| [THEORY-390](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-390.md) | Any distribution of n × N matrices whose norms concentrate as Johnson–Lindenstrauss proofs require gives the restricted isometry property of order k with probability at least 1 − 2e^{−c₂n} for k ≤ c₁n/log(N/k), by a union bound over (12/δ)^k net points on each of the (eN/k)^k sparse supports; this makes k log(N/k) measurements sufficient for Gaussian, ±1 and sparse three-valued matrices, and does not show they are necessary | Baraniuk, Davenport, DeVore and Wakin (2008), [LIT-1156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1156.md), read in [NOTE-931](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-931.md) from the author-posted copy. The only assumption is the concentration inequality Pr(\|‖Φx‖² − ‖x‖²\| ≥ ε‖x‖²) ≤ 2e^{−nc₀(ε)}, met with Achlioptas's c₀(ε) = ε²/4 − ε³/6. The proof is the JL argument run over a net on every sparse support, plus a step from the net to the whole subspace. Necessity of k log(N/k) is recalled from Gelfand widths, not derived from concentration, and constants are implicit. | Active |
| [THEORY-392](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-392.md) v2 | Every map from an n-point subset of a metric space into Hilbert space extends to the whole space with Lipschitz constant at most K√(log n) times its own, by dimension reduction to K log n coordinates followed by Kirszbraun and the non-linear Hahn–Banach theorem; for L_p, 1 ≤ p < 2, the constant must be at least δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/p−1/2), so √(log n) is right up to a log log factor in the worst case | Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md). Theorem 1 proves Marcus and Pisier's conjecture L(X, n) ≤ K(Log n)^(1/2) for every metric space X; Theorem 3 gives L(p, n) ≥ δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/p−1/2) for 1 ≤ p < 2, hence L(∞, n) ≥ δ(Log n/Log Log n)^(1/2). The √(log n) comes from the √k cost of passing between ℓ₂ᵏ and ℓ∞ᵏ, with k of order log n. Whether the upper bound is sharp the paper leaves open, and the constants are loose. | Active |
| [THEORY-393](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-393.md) | Any two families of n vectors of norm at most 1 have images in ⌊C log(2 + ε²n)/ε²⌋ dimensions whose cross inner products ⟨x_i, y_j⟩ are each within an additive ε of the originals, found by a randomized polynomial-time algorithm, which for small ε is below the log n/ε² of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma; only cross products are kept, the new vectors' norms are not bounded, and whether one set can be embedded that small is open | Alon and Klartag (2017), [LIT-1151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1151.md), read in [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) from arXiv v4. Theorem 1.2 answers, in a bipartite form, Larsen and Nelson's question whether log n can become log(2 + ε²n) in the JL lemma. The proof is convex geometry: Khatri–Šidák bounds the Gaussian measure of a body of slabs, and a weakened low M*-estimate puts a random t-dimensional subspace close to every scaled a_i. Conjecture 2.4, the same with norms O(1), is proved only for t of order n (Theorem 2.5). It is not an embedding of one point set and says nothing about distances. | Active |
| [THEORY-394](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-394.md) | Every n-point metric space embeds in Euclidean space of O(log n) dimensions with distortion O(log n), by distances to random sets of every scale followed by Johnson–Lindenstrauss, and constant-degree expanders need distortion Ω(log n) in every ℓ_p with 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, so O(log n) is tight in the worst case; the constants are unspecified, the lower bound rests on Leighton and Rao's flow–cut gap, and nothing is shown for trees or for p > 2 | Linial, London and Rabinovich (1995), [LIT-1155](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1155.md), read in [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) from the authors' February 1995 manuscript. Theorem 3.2(1) states Bourgain's theorem ([LIT-1161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1161.md), unread): every n-point metric embeds in O(log n)-dimensional Euclidean space with distortion O(log n). The paper reproves the distortion with a randomized map into ℓ_p^{O(log² n)} built from distances to O(log n) random sets of each size 2ˡ, and gets the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss. Proposition 4.2 shows that every embedding of a constant-degree expander into ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, has distortion Ω(log n), from the expander's Ω(log n) gap between flow and cut. Together these answer Johnson and Lindenstrauss's Problem 4 in the negative, which the paper does not say. | Active |
| [THEORY-395](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-395.md) v2 | For ε between about lg^0.5001 n/√min{n, d} and 1, some n-point set in ℝ^d needs Ω(ε⁻² lg(ε²n)) dimensions under any map, linear or not, that keeps its pairwise squared distances within 1 ± ε, so a random projection with a union bound is optimal up to a constant for the worst set; nearly orthogonal sets can need fewer, and the bound says nothing about typical data | Larsen and Nelson (2017), [LIT-1154](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1154.md), read in [NOTE-925](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-925.md) from arXiv v2. Theorem 2 removes the lg(1/ε) gap that Welch, Levenshtein and Alon left, for arbitrary maps. The proof is an encoding argument over a family of k-sparse vectors with k ≈ ε⁻², ending at nm = Ω(kn lg(d/k)). It is a worst-case bound by existence with an untracked constant. It is not a phase transition, and the paper notes that ε-incoherent sets fit in o(ε⁻² lg n) dimensions for small enough ε. | Active |
| [THEORY-396](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-396.md) | Every Lipschitz map from an n-point metric space into any Banach space extends to any containing space with Lipschitz constant at most C log n/log log n times its own, by averaging over random partitions at every scale, and every n-point subset of L₂ extends into any Banach space at C√(log n) after Johnson–Lindenstrauss dimension reduction; for maps into Hilbert space this is no improvement on K√(log n), and whether √(log n) suffices for every target is left open | Lee and Naor (2005), [LIT-1152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1152.md), read in [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) from the authors' January 2004 preprint. Theorem 1.10 (Theorem 5.1(4)): ae(X) ≤ C log n/log log n for every n-point metric space X, bounding the extension constant over every superspace and every Banach target at once, improving Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's C log n. Theorem 1.12: eₙ(L_p, Z) ≤ C(p)(log n)^{1/p} for 1 < p ≤ 2, C√(log n) at p = 2, through the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma and e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d. For Hilbert targets Johnson and Lindenstrauss's K√(log n) ([THEORY-392](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-392.md)) stays the better bound, and the paper states as open whether O(√(log n)) holds for every metric domain and normed target. | Active |
| [THEORY-397](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-397.md) | A random linear map into k ≥ 4(ε²/2 − ε³/3)⁻¹ ln n dimensions keeps every pairwise squared distance of a fixed set of n points in ℓ₂ within 1 ± ε, because each difference vector's squared length concentrates with tails exp(−(k/2)(ε²/2 − ε³/3)) and a union bound over the pairs costs only ln n; the proofs cover a random subspace, Gaussian entries and independent zero-mean ±1 or √3·{+1, 0, −1} entries, and no matrix with nonnegative entries | Dasgupta and Gupta (2003), [LIT-1157](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1157.md), read in [NOTE-932](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-932.md), give the explicit bound for a projection onto a random subspace; Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md), prove the lemma with k = [K(τ) log n] and K ≥ (10/τ)² by Lévy's isoperimetric inequality; Achlioptas, [LIT-1159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1159.md), read in [NOTE-926](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-926.md) from a 2002 draft, carries the same k₀ to independent ±1 and sparse three-valued entries. The guarantee is for a fixed finite set, on squared distances, and it rests on entries being zero-mean. It says nothing about maps that go up in dimension or are followed by a threshold. | Active |
| [THEORY-398](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-398.md) v2 | A Lipschitz map from a subset of a metric space whose points are at least ε apart and whose diameter is D extends to the whole space into Hilbert space with Lipschitz constant at most 6D/ε times its own, and, by Benyamini's argument in the same paper, into any Banach space with at most 4D/ε, with no dependence on the number of points | Johnson and Lindenstrauss (1984), [LIT-1153](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1153.md), read in [NOTE-930](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-930.md). Theorem 2 gives 6D/ε for maps into ℓ₂, through ℓ₁ and a weak form of Grothendieck's inequality; Benyamini's appendix gives 4D/ε for any Banach target, through a retraction of ℓ∞(Γ) with Lipschitz constant at most 2. The bound trades the count of points for the spread of the set. Whether either constant is best possible is not discussed. | Active |
| [THEORY-399](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-399.md) | Storing every inner product of n points of the unit ball of R^k to additive error ε takes Θ(n log n/ε²) bits once k ≥ log n/ε² and Θ(nk log(2 + log n/(ε²k))) below, for 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1, and comparing these counts across dimensions shows that some n such points cannot be mapped into fewer than Ω(min{k, log(2 + ε²n)/ε²}) dimensions with additive error ε for every ε ≥ 2/√n; this is a worst-case lower bound with unstated constants, the small-ε bit count is open for k above that dimension, and no one-family embedding that small is proved | Alon and Klartag (2017), [LIT-1151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1151.md), read in [NOTE-929](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-929.md) from arXiv v4. Theorem 1.1 gives the bits of an additive ε-distance sketch for every k when 1/n^0.49 ≤ ε ≤ 0.1, by a volume argument above and a packing of net points against random probes below. Since an embedding is a sketch, Corollary 2.1 re-proves Larsen and Nelson's bound in that range, and Corollary 2.3, using the Gaussian correlation inequality in place of a union bound, extends it to every ε ≥ 2/√n with log(2 + ε²n) in place of log n. The dimension statements are for additive error on squared distances of points of norm at most 1; the relative form for small ε follows but is not stated. The matching upper bound for one set is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-400](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-400.md) | A metric space that admits, at every scale, random partitions into small pieces with each point padded away from piece boundaries with constant probability is absolutely Lipschitz extendable: maps from it into any Banach space extend to any containing space at O(1/padding), which gives C log λ for doubling constant λ, C r² for K_r-minor-free graph metrics, C(g+1) on genus-g surfaces and C√d from ℓ₂ᵈ; the bounds are upper bounds only, and the method needs a decomposition the domain may not have | Lee and Naor (2005), [LIT-1152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1152.md), read in [NOTE-927](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-927.md) from the authors' January 2004 preprint. Theorem 4.1 turns (ε, δ)-padded random partitions of the domain at every scale into a C/(εδ)-gentle partition of unity, and Lemma 2.1 turns that into extensions of constant 3C/(εδ) into any Banach space; Lemma 3.8 carries the partitions from X to any superspace. Theorem 5.1 gives ae(X) ≤ C log λ(X), ≤ C r² for K_r-minor-free graph metrics, ≤ C(g+1) on surfaces of genus g, and e(ℓ₂ᵈ, Z) ≤ C√d, generalizing Johnson, Lindenstrauss and Schechtman's Cd and Matoušek's trees. No lower bound shows any of them tight. | Active |
